"Already tried them; they have a ten-sheet minimum, and I'm on a graduate-student budget. Would 150 gsm cotton rag handle a lino-print cover, or would it crack along the fold?" He tapped the thumbnail mockup sitting between them; the fold line had already worn into a faint scar.

"Borrowing bone folders feels harmless until they audit the lab. Maybe just buy one and charge it to 'research'?" Her phone screen glowed; she silenced it without looking.

"Feed grain direction—should it run spinewise or cross-grain for saddle stitch?" He felt his next heartbeat catch somewhere in his throat.

"Honestly? By the time you're obsessing over grain, the reader is licking tahini off her fingers. Just pick whatever folds flattest through the toner." She stepped to the side, her coat sweeping through the light from the cracked window.

"Fair point. If none of it works, do you think the library printer could color-scan the originals front and back?" He tried to make the question sound offhand.

"The library printer jams on cardstock; it'll chew up your granny's ink and sneer. I really have to go—the bus leaves in two." She was already past the espresso machine before the final syllable landed. The rectangle of cold glass snapped back into the space where she'd been, and Yusuf noticed, at last, that the steam had truly disappeared.

The fluorescent lights buzzed above, electricity humming its steady tune while the ink on the weekly safety poster surrendered slowly to nothing. Khalisa rocked from foot to foot, a USB stick pinched between her fingers like a charm warding off administrative limbo. The parking meter outside was down to perhaps twenty minutes, and she'd already made two laps through these corridors this week fighting over IRB footnotes.

Simonette occupied the space behind the counter, sleeves pushed up, her coffee mug professing loyalty to deprecated storage formats. She plucked a jelly bean from the consent jar—red on this occasion—and gestured for Khalisa to go ahead.

"Level with me—does this data-sharing agreement protect us if the vendor gets hacked?"

"That hinges on what you mean by hacked. The clause requires them to maintain 'industry-standard technical safeguards'—which is flannel unless they name specific standards."

Khalisa's shoulders crept upward. "Wonderful, so flannel. How do I stomp on that?"

"Ask them to cite NIST 800-53 controls or equivalent; if they refuse, red flag."

"I already asked. They sent back a line about 'reasonable efforts.' That's more fluff."

Simonette's pen scraped across a sticky note. "Counteroffer: strike 'reasonable,' insert 'in accordance with,' then append their SOC-2 report date."

The binders propped against the wall stood as patient witnesses to every prior crisis. Khalisa's eyes flicked toward them, then returned to Simonette. "Assume they sign that. Do I still need local backups for re-identification risk?"

"We demand two mirrored encrypted drives stored on campus, no exceptions. Give IRB that wording verbatim and they'll smile."

"Okay, encryption at rest—AES-256 or just AES?"

"Spell out AES-256, FIPS 140-3 certified. Vendors try shaving bits to save licensing fees."

Khalisa jotted something down. "What if participant IDs leak downstream? Who's liable?"

"Page four, indemnification section: they shoulder up to the amount of the research grant or actual damages, whichever's lower. You're capped at your budget, so again, local backups mitigate that."

The jelly beans rattled as Simonette fished out another one. Khalisa's parking meter was likely in single digits by now. "Automatic deletion period—should we push for five or ten years?"

"Ten if you plan meta-analyses; five if storage costs kill you. Either way, hard delete, not 'logical,' with audit letter to prove it."

"The vendor wants broad 'research purposes' language. Too broad?"

"Strike it, add 'solely for the purposes described in Protocol #2024-77,' plus the PI's name. Keeps their lawyers from repurposing your scans for marketing."

Khalisa tapped her pen on the counter. "Still feels like holes. Anything missing?"

"Sidecar term—require them to notify you within 24 hours of any data incident. Email and phone, not just ticketing system."

"You've got jelly-bean logic; write that clause for me?"

"Already drafting. Bring your stamp and you're parking-meter-safe."

Borisla hunched on the mezzanine grate, her nose long since gone numb, and stared at the copper sprinkler line that had transformed itself into forty feet of what looked like a holiday popsicle. "Half this line's a popsicle," she shouted down to the figure leaning against the post. "How am I supposed to check whether it's split without thawing it?" Her advisor wanted failure data; standing around up here wasn't writing the thesis.

Edda pushed herself away from the salt bucket, her clipboard swinging like an unripe fruit from her hand. "Tap along the copper with a small wrench; listen for a dull hollow knock instead of solid metal." The pen's red string trembled in the downdraft.

"Tap and pray—that's the whole plan?" Borisla unclipped the wrench from her belt; the orange lanyard caught on her glove, then snapped free.

"Pretty much. Split ice sounds like cracked glass under the skin. Then feel for soft copper—freeze bulges are usually near couplings."

A flash of memory—professors, endless delays—flickered through Borisla's mind. "If it's bulged, do I cut?"

"Don't cut. Just mark it with tape, photograph it, and log the circumference with seamstress tape if you carry one." Edda flexed her fingers, quiet amusement visible only in the crinkles at the corners of her eyes.

Borisla glanced at the cracked bucket of salt. "Rock salt bucket's here. Safe to use on the ice?"

"Don't use it. Salt takes hours and flakes the copper. After it warms we'll pulse the dry-valve once to relieve pressure; then you record flow gauge."

"I need my co-author for the gauge—he's good at timing leaks. Anything else before thaw?"

"Note ambient temp, exact hour crew evacuated, and if you smell antifreeze in the drip cup below—that tells us glycol enclosure failed upstream."

Borisla pictured the cup bolted to the bottom of the main. "Antifreeze smell like sweet cough syrup?"

"Exactly. One part in fifty air, one whiff does it. You'll know."

"Okay." She slid the wrench into her pocket and steadied her feet on the slick grate. "I'll tap, look, snap photos, then wait for clearance. Pens up here freeze too; mind if I borrow that red string as tie-off?"

"Go ahead. Clip it to your zipper pull so it doesn't blow into the grate cracks." Edda backed toward the ladder, calm as if she'd been asked for the time. "Call me when you're done."

Borisla nodded—minimalist, impatient—and knelt. She tapped the first length of pipe. The sound of metal answered, sharp and intact, as skylight snow whispered down through the frosted glass onto her shoulders.

The fluorescent tube above aisle fourteen stuttered through its seven-second asylum flicker just as Hana walked beneath it, her running shoes speckled with the residue of two semesters' worth of test whites. "Hi — the websites all contradict each other," she said, polite but already wound tight. "I need anchors that can hold a twenty-two-pound mirror on drywall. Which of these boxes do I actually grab?"

Felix stood up straight and tapped the carton with a dusty knuckle. "Grab the yellow ones labeled 'self-drilling steel anchors—50 lb.' They spread behind the wall like little wings and won't tear out."

Hana's eyebrows rose like they had mileage to burn. "Wings sound great, but my wall's only half-inch drywall above a strip of… something harder. Plaster maybe. Same anchors still OK?"

"Quarter-inch pilot — got it." Hana turned the box over; the instructions seemed to be trying to escape under the HVAC sigh. "Do I need the drill bit this store sells or will my roommate's mismatched junk drawer work?"

Felix's smile lived mostly in his eyes. "Junk drawer bit works if it's sharp; steel cares about spin speed and pressure more than brand. Dull bit just makes angry dust."

"Separate aisle. Grab the two-inch Phillips heads hanging on the strip right of the drill bits; same thread, same finish, and you'll still clear the glass hook plate."

"You've probably just saved me another migraine." Hana turned the little bag he handed her over in her hands; thirty ounces of metal had never looked so cooperative. "Anything else I'll curse myself for forgetting at one in the morning?"

The radio droned something about open roads at half its usual pace while sunlight oozed through the cracked window like slow honey. "Heat it with a hair dryer, then burnish with a credit card. The adhesive sets smoother when warm."

The iron shed carried the smell of diesel fuel and damp rock. Camille's boots ground against the gritty floor as she entered, the paper template of her sentence—*May memory bloom with every season*—folded in her hand like a letter with no address.

Einar kept his eyes on the sandwich he was working through before the next person bothered him. "Wrong table. Maintenance farms that work out to the city yard. Try the guild over on River Street."

Isak's notebook—its pages already blistering—snapped shut. "Thanks, Apiarist Anonymous. Could you stick to hygroscopic substrates?"

"Bees collect propolis to coat cavity walls; thin resin layer resists microbes—paint the back of your shelves with that zeal."

Nerea's shattered phone lay across the hood of the hatchback like a broken mirror, catching the stutter of the failing overhead light. Chalk marks from rehearsal haunted the concrete below; three minutes and five seconds of rooftop footage burned inside the fractured screen. "Hey, got a second before you head out?" she called, jogging between the idling van and the pillar. "I need a straight opinion on a single-take audition clip, and word is you speak cut better than you speak English."

Jareth's fingers were already bleached white around his key fob, hoodie only half zipped, exhaust curling around his shins. "If it's a locked take, you're finished, right? One-take means there are no cuts left to hunt for."

"The piece runs three-oh-five; the judges want three flat. Somewhere in that I'm supposed to disappear for four heartbeats."

He scratched at a phantom itch beneath his cuff. "Four beats is simple—mute the backing track for two counts, fades the problem into the floor."

The senior center carried its usual December stench—cinnamon so thick it felt radioactive, and instant coffee that stained your tongue the shade of bargain carpet. Folding tables bowed beneath everyone's nostalgia craft: cookie-cutter stars, dented pie tins, the unavoidable pipe-cleaner candy cane. Gul sat hunched over a six-inch square of roofing tin scavenged from a storm, sleeves pushed up high, black prints across his fingers where the metal had fought back. Across the vinyl snowflakes, Hristo held a leaking reindeer mug as though it contained classified information. Gul skipped pleasantries entirely. "I need it to catch light like a mirror, but every time I fold the edges they stay sharp enough to cut skin. How do I fix that without losing the shine?"

Hristo kept his eyes down. "You're folding once and stopping. Do a double fold, quarter inch in, then flatten the seam with the flat face of the hammer. That kills the edge and buries the burr."

Gul's eyebrow twitched—a single beat of impatience. "Won't that destroy the crisp line? I'm after a snowflake—details smaller than an eighth of an inch."

Hristo smiled for the first time, barely, like a man who'd just realized he enjoyed the song playing overhead. "The crisp line holds if you score it first. Use the ball-peen to mark the inside score, then bend along that score with needle-nose pliers. The metal obeys the rule instead of your thumbs guessing." He mimed the motions with empty hands, wrists loose, muscle memory doing the talking.

Gul angled the tin, checking reflections only a calculus major would bother with. "What about the reflection? A folded edge blocks half the angle."

"The fold sits on the back. The front face remains flat." Hristo tapped the table twice to drive the point home. "After the fold, take a 320-grit sponge, light circles, six passes—removes the micro-burr and gives you polish."

"Skip the sponge on the texture zones." Hristo reached for a roll of blue painter's tape and tore off a sliver with absent-minded precision. "Mask it with tape cut to the silhouette, polish around it, peel it off when you're done."

Hristo raised the reindeer mug in a gesture too fluid to be a toast and too final to be a brush-off. "Grinding eats tin thickness faster than rust does. Keep the hammer singing and the tin behaves."

Up front, the glue guns sputtered awake. Neither of them reached for them yet; the tin in Gul's hand, beneath the tired December light, was finally behaving.

The afternoon sun lays thin stripes across the cutting board, where an IT8 target is taped down like a garish ransom note. "New reference file. Pull the 30% gray patch, subtract 3 in 'b', re-export the .ti1."

Theocharis shrugs his pack off again, ready for this final stop. "Tick 'custom perceptual' on the last line, date it, and you're covered." He gives up the chair; she slides into its residual warmth.

Jasmina shoved a plastic chair in Levent's direction with the heel of her boot, the legs scraping harshly across the canvas ground. "I've got seconds-granular skin temperature data burying me alive—how do I boil it down to a single red flag per firefighter?"

Levent perched his laptop on one knee, the cooler beneath him wobbling like a stool that resented being sat on. "Start with a rolling maximum across ninety-second windows, then flag anything sitting two standard deviations above that person's own pre-drill baseline. Gives you a clean binary go or no-go."

She tapped the trackpad, rows of data scrolling past faster than her heartbeat. "Fine, except two sigma lights up half the crew during an Alabama summer. I need better specificity."

He grinned, clearly delighted that a theory had held up against the real world. "Simple—raise the threshold to three sigma and also require a sustained trend lasting three minutes; that caps false positives unless the sun is actively trying to kill them."

"Right, but the fog of post-exercise suppression throws off the baseline—how do I separate that out?"

Levent tapped the lid of her laptop. "Discard the first five minutes after they exit, wait for heart rate to fall below one-ten; whatever shows up after that is genuine heat load, not an anxiety spike."

"Tag it as a 'cooling period,' strip it from the slope calculation; use hydration timestamps as masks, expect mean reversion within two minutes, ignore it."

Jasmina looked over at a table where half-filled cups stood in a jagged skyline. "I only logged water at the bucket level, not individual sips; there are gaps in the data."

"Interpolate between the hydration events you do have—linear interpolation is fine, this isn't an ICU study—then slap a low-confidence flag on any questionable windows and review them manually later."

The word manually sank into her like a bruise. "Manual means me sitting here at two a.m.—I need a filter that auto-excludes obvious sensor dropouts too."

"Easy dropouts are any reading that jumps ten degrees in a single second—censor the adjacent five-second buffer, take a majority vote across the three nearest sensors to patch the gap."

She let out a breath, a small win. "Grand. Once I have clean flags, should I average them or take the worst episode per shift?"

He leaned back, palms resting on his thighs. "For policy uplink: worst single sustained episode per individual. Regulations love absolute peaks, not convoluted means."

"Output just that timestamp, value, and individual ID—CSV line? JSON?"

"CSV, three columns. Chiefs open it in Excel like sacred scripture. Deliver it nightly via sftp to the 'Rehab Dashboard' folder—it's already whitelisted."

She laughed, the sound catching both of them off guard above the hiss of the leaking hose, and snapped the band shut on her clipboard.

The back office smelled like old fryer grease and the adhesive holding down the carpet edges. "Hey Nirmala—got a couple of minutes? I'm trying to put together a soft launch plan for the digital menu rollout."

"Colin's away on vacation till Thursday. I keep running into walls with phased deployments. Can you at least tell me whether there's a standard trail-store sequence?"

"Sure, but there's got to be a risk matrix somewhere. Older POS units first, then the high-volume ones?"

"Ask Marketing—I just move tomatoes from A to B."

"That was an emergency inventory salvage. Totally different animal."

"Even so, you must recall whether the Riverfront branch went down during peak lunch. That's usable intel."

The edge of her tote bag squeaked against the chair. "All I remember is we ran out of jalapeños by Tuesday."

"I don't have ticket access. I'm literally capped at spreadsheets full of apples."

A shrug. "Honestly? Venue tech. But half of them are contractors and the other half are at a conference in Vegas. Hashtag sorry."

"One last thing—can I at least screengrab the past three months of sales by hour from your dashboard? That's neutral territory."

Her hand was already on the doorframe as she delivered the final deflection. "Dashboard auto-wipes at end of cycle. Nothing to grab. Try Finance?"

Bastian watched the foamcore menus tremble overhead, listened to the hallway echo of jalapeño crates being counted, and wondered whether anyone in this place worried about software half as much as they worried about vegetables.

The corner grocer was barely larger than a walk-in closet, its strip light buzzing overhead while cilantro wilted in its plastic wrapping. Low orange sunlight seeped through the glass front. Ramadan began tomorrow, and the tight aisles pulsed with last-minute shoppers and their carts.

Behind the counter, Ibtisam was stacking ful tins like bricks, the brim of her cap casting shadow over her eyes. The wall clock gave her forty-one minutes—forty-one minutes of "Sure, we have that" before her ride might pull away from the curb.

Steam rolled over the gravel in a slow, purposeful wave, carrying the smell of straw and used espresso into both their faces. Sofiane narrowed his eyes against it. The compost windrows lay like sleeping dragons, and his coil rig waited in their shade, ready for holes that would only land in the right spots if someone handed him precise numbers. Diesel fumes and the sharp metallic ticking of cooling welds drifted into the half-open bay on the wind coming off the water. Jolene stood beside the wheel well of a gutted transit bus, her dented clipboard pressed against her coat like a piece of armor that had already let her down. A single page of figures was due tomorrow; her advisor wanted a heat-load number, not a story. She had already tried three online calculators, and each one had handed her a different wrong answer.

Sameer slid out from beneath the chassis on a creeper, his tools rattling against his hips. A cold drop fell from the chrome chase overhead and trickled down inside his collar. He looked up at Jolene's boots, took in the way she was shivering, and resolved to keep this brief.

Her pen hung in the air. "You've already lost me. Can you just give me BTUs?"

"Fair enough. Interior surface area of the shell is around eight-twenty square feet; we use a delta-T of thirty degrees—forty-five outside, a comfortable seventy-five inside. 820 times .077 times 30 gets you one-nine-hundred BTU."

"That's only the shell?"

"Plus. The fridge draws two-fifty watts while running, that's another eight-fifty BTU."

"Thirty-five fifty—does the lighting factor in?"

"Six T8 LED tubes at thirty-five watts apiece; add two-hundred on top, barely makes a dent."

"And solar load—the sun beating on it?"

"Fifteen is generous. Grab the twelve K motor and sleep easy."
